claims.text: What the image looks like Intraluminal filling defect in a pulmonary artery (CT-PA) → pulmonary embolism (gold standard)
claims.quote: Intraluminal filling defect in pulmonary artery (CT-PA) Pulmonary embolism (gold standard)

claims.text: Example CTA: bilateral pulmonary embolism; the filling defects are the emboli
claims.quote: The images show bilateral pulmonary embolism on chest computed tomographic angiography. The arrows point to the filling defects (emboli).

claims.text: Buzzword: Westermark sign (focal oligemia) on CXR → pulmonary embolism
claims.quote: Westermark sign (focal oligemia) CXR Pulmonary embolism

claims.text: V/Q scan: ventilation/perfusion mismatch (perfusion defect with normal ventilation) = high probability PE; use when CT-PA is contraindicated (renal failure, contrast allergy, pregnancy)
claims.quote: V/Q scan Ventilation/perfusion mismatch (perfusion defect with normal ventilation) = high probability PE Use when CT-PA contraindicated (renal failure, contrast allergy, pregnancy)

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) CT angiography is the preferred imaging technique for acute PE: rapid, accurate, and highly sensitive and specific
claims.quote: CT angiography is the preferred imaging technique for diagnosing acute pulmonary embolism. It is rapid, accurate, and highly sensitive and specific.

claims.text: CTA also shows other lung pathology (eg, pneumonia rather than PE) and PE severity (eg, by the size of the right ventricle or reflux into the hepatic veins)
claims.quote: It can also give more information about other lung pathology (eg, demonstration of pneumonia rather than PE as a cause of hypoxia or pleuritic chest pain) as well as severity of PE (for example by the size of the right ventricle or the reflux into the hepatic veins).

claims.text: Sensitivity is highest for emboli in the main pulmonary artery or lobar or segmental vessels, and lowest for subsegmental emboli (about 30% of all PEs)
claims.quote: The sensitivity of CT angiography is highest for pulmonary embolism in the main pulmonary artery or lobar or segmental vessels. Sensitivity of CT angiography is lowest for emboli in subsegmental vessels (about 30% of all pulmonary emboli).

claims.text: CXR (insensitive): Westermark sign (focal oligemia) / Hampton hump (wedge pleural-based opacity) → get CTPA or V/Q scan
claims.quote: Westermark sign (focal oligemia) / Hampton hump (wedge pleural-based opacity) Pulmonary embolism (CXR insensitive) Get CTPA or V/Q scan
claims.locator: Chest X-Ray (CXR), Cardiac / Vascular / PE table

claims.text: Hampton hump = pleural-based wedge (peripheral infarct)
claims.quote: Hampton hump (pleural-based wedge) CXR Pulmonary embolism (peripheral infarct)

claims.text: The CXR is usually nonspecific (atelectasis, focal infiltrates, elevated hemidiaphragm, pleural effusion); Westermark sign, Hampton hump or an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery are suggestive but uncommon (insensitive) and have low specificity
claims.quote: The chest radiograph usually is nonspecific but may show atelectasis, focal infiltrates, an elevated hemidiaphragm, or a pleural effusion. The classic findings of focal loss of vascular markings (Westermark sign), a peripheral, wedge-shaped density arising from the pleura (Hampton hump), or enlargement of the right descending pulmonary artery are suggestive but uncommon (ie, insensitive) and have low specificity.

claims.text: V/Q scan: detects lung areas that are ventilated but not perfused; highly sensitive when the CXR is normal or near normal with no significant underlying lung disease
claims.quote: Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scans in pulmonary embolism detect areas of lung that are ventilated but not perfused. V/Q scanning takes much longer than CT angiography and is less specific. However, when chest radiograph findings are normal or near normal and no significant underlying lung disease exists, it is a highly sensitive test.

claims.text: V/Q is particularly useful when renal insufficiency precludes contrast, and in pregnancy
claims.quote: V/Q scanning is particularly useful when renal insufficiency precludes the use of contrast agents, which are otherwise required for CT angiography, and in patients who are pregnant (6).

claims.text: Causes Nearly all pulmonary emboli arise from thrombi in the veins of the legs or pelvis (DVT); risk of embolization is higher with thrombi that reach the popliteal vein or above
claims.quote: Nearly all pulmonary emboli arise from thrombi in the veins of the legs or pelvis (deep venous thrombosis). Risk of embolization is higher with thrombi that reach the popliteal vein or above.

claims.text: Nonthrombotic sources: air, amniotic fluid, fat, infected material, orthopedic cement, foreign body, tumor
claims.quote: Pulmonary embolism can also arise from nonthrombotic sources (eg, embolism of air, amniotic fluid, fat, infected material, orthopedic cement, foreign body, tumor).

claims.text: Risk factors: conditions that impair venous return, conditions that cause endothelial injury or dysfunction, and underlying hypercoagulable states
claims.quote: Risk factors for pulmonary embolism are conditions that impair venous return, conditions that cause endothelial injury or dysfunction, and underlying hypercoagulable states.

claims.text: Symptoms Many emboli are small, physiologically insignificant and asymptomatic; symptoms are nonspecific
claims.quote: Many pulmonary emboli are small, physiologically insignificant, and asymptomatic. Even when present, symptoms are nonspecific and vary in frequency and intensity, depending on the extent of pulmonary vascular occlusion and preexisting cardiopulmonary function.

claims.text: Often: acute dyspnea; pleuritic chest pain (when there is pulmonary infarction)
claims.quote: Emboli often cause Acute dyspnea Pleuritic chest pain (when there is pulmonary infarction)

claims.text: Less common: cough; hemoptysis (occasionally, with pulmonary infarction); in older patients the first symptom may be altered mental status
claims.quote: Less common symptoms include Cough (usually caused by comorbid disorders or by dilation of the pulmonary arteries) Hemoptysis (occasionally occurs when there is pulmonary infarction) In older patients, the first symptom may be altered mental status.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: anticoagulation (LMWH/DOAC); thrombolysis if hemodynamically unstable
claims.quote: Anticoagulation (LMWH/DOAC); thrombolysis if hemodynamically unstable

claims.text: Anticoagulation is the mainstay; thrombolytic therapy or embolectomy is indicated for hypotension that does not resolve after fluid resuscitation, and for selected patients with impaired RV function or escalating oxygen requirements
claims.quote: Anticoagulation is the mainstay of therapy for PE. Rapid reduction of clot burden via thrombolytic therapy or embolectomy is indicated for patients with hypotension that does not resolve after fluid resuscitation, and for selected patients with impaired RV function or escalating oxygen requirements.

claims.text: Because anticoagulation improves survival, give anticoagulants when PE is diagnosed or strongly suspected
claims.quote: Because anticoagulation improves survival, patients should be given anticoagulants when PE is diagnosed or strongly suspected.
